questions.prompt: What is `std::array<T, N>`'s object representation?
options: An aggregate whose entire representation is one `T[N]` member, so it is standard-layout and trivially copyable whenever `T` is.
A class holding a `T*` to a heap block plus a stored size, so `sizeof` is 16 bytes on x86-64 for any `N`.
An aggregate holding a `T[N]` plus a cached size member, so `sizeof` is slightly larger than `N * sizeof(T)`.
A class with a defaulted constructor and an allocator member, so it is standard-layout but never trivially copyable.
questions.explanation: `std::array` is a plain aggregate over a raw array and holds nothing else, which is why `sizeof(std::array<int,8>) == 32` and why it can be `memcpy`'d, placed in shared memory, or used as a C++20 NTTP. The 'array plus a size member' answer is the tempting one — the size is a template parameter, known at compile time, so there is nothing to store. There is no allocator and no indirection: the elements *are* the object.

questions.prompt: At block scope, how do `std::array<int,3> a;` and `std::array<int,3> b{};` differ?
options: `a`'s elements are default-initialized and therefore indeterminate; `b`'s are value-initialized and therefore all zero.
Both forms value-initialize the elements to zero; the braces are redundant for a trivial element type.
`a`'s elements are zeroed and `b`'s are indeterminate, since braces suppress initialization of the inner array.
`a` is ill-formed because an aggregate has no default constructor, so the braced form is the only valid one.
questions.explanation: Default-initializing an aggregate of trivial type initializes nothing, so reading `a[0]` reads garbage; the empty braces value-initialize and zero everything. 'Both are zero' is the common belief and comes from confusing block scope with namespace scope, where static storage duration would zero-initialize either way. The braces are the whole difference here, not decoration.

questions.prompt: What is the status of `std::array<int, 0> z;`?
options: Valid: `empty()` is true, `begin() == end()`, `data()` may return null, and calling `front()` is undefined behavior.
Ill-formed, because a zero-length array member is not valid C++ and is only a GNU extension.
Valid, and `front()` returns a reference to a single value-initialized element kept for exactly this case.
Valid, but `begin()` and `end()` compare unequal because `data()` is required to return a non-null pointer.
questions.explanation: The zero-size specialization is one of the concrete wins over `T[N]`, where `int x[0]` is ill-formed and only compiles as a GNU extension. It behaves as a proper empty range — the iterators compare equal — but `front()` and `back()` still dereference nothing and are UB, which is the part people forget once they hear 'it's valid'. `data()` is permitted to return null.

questions.prompt: What do mainstream `std::vector` implementations store, and what is `sizeof(std::vector<int>)` on x86-64?
options: Three pointers — buffer start, one-past-last-element, one-past-buffer-end — giving 24 bytes.
A buffer pointer plus `size_t` size and `size_t` capacity, which is what libstdc++ and libc++ actually use, giving 24 bytes.
A buffer pointer plus a `size_t` size, with capacity queried from the allocator, giving 16 bytes.
Four pointers — start, end, capacity end, and a cached allocator handle — giving 32 bytes.
questions.explanation: libstdc++, libc++, and MSVC all use pointer triples, from which `size()` and `capacity()` are subtractions. The size/capacity pair is the tempting distractor because it occupies the same 24 bytes and is how people imagine the class — but it costs an extra add on every dereference, which is exactly why pointers won. Allocators are typically empty and take no space via EBO.

questions.prompt: `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<T>> v;` — `v.emplace_back(new T);` compiles while `v.push_back(new T);` does not. Why?
options: `emplace_back` direct-initializes the element, which can select `unique_ptr`'s `explicit` constructor; `push_back` needs an implicit conversion, which `explicit` forbids.
`push_back` takes its argument by `const&` only, so a prvalue pointer has nothing to bind to, whereas `emplace_back` forwards an rvalue.
`emplace_back` is a template and templates are exempt from `explicit` constructor checks during overload resolution.
`push_back` requires the element to be copy-constructible, which `unique_ptr` is not; `emplace_back` requires only move-construction.
questions.explanation: The direct- vs copy-initialization difference is the whole story, and it makes `emplace_back(new T)` a leak hazard: if the growth allocation throws, the raw pointer is never adopted, so prefer `emplace_back(std::make_unique<T>())`. The copy-constructible answer is the seductive one — `push_back` has a `T&&` overload and works fine with `std::move`d unique_ptrs, so copyability is not the obstacle.

questions.prompt: Why does `std::vector<bool>` break generic code?
options: It is a bit-packed specialization: `operator[]` returns a proxy object, there is no `data()`, and `auto x = v[0]` deduces the proxy rather than `bool`.
It stores one `bool` per byte like `vector<char>` but specializes only its comparison operators, which breaks `std::equal`.
It packs bits yet still returns `bool&` from `operator[]`, so `&v[0]` yields a `bool*` into the middle of a packed word.
It is an ordinary container whose allocator is specialized to a bit-packing one, so only allocator-aware code is affected.
questions.explanation: The proxy reference is the defect: it cannot be bound to `bool&`, there is no addressable `bool` to point at, and `auto` silently captures the proxy so the value changes underneath you. The `bool*` answer is self-contradictory once you see it — you cannot take the address of a single bit, which is precisely why the proxy exists. Use `vector<char>`, `vector<uint8_t>`, or `std::bitset`.

questions.prompt: With `v.size() == v.capacity()`, what is the status of `v.push_back(v[0]);`?
options: Well-defined: the standard requires implementations to construct the new element before the old buffer is released.
Undefined behavior, because reallocation frees the old buffer and the reference `v[0]` dangles before the copy happens.
Well-defined only if you `reserve` beforehand; without spare capacity it is undefined behavior.
Well-defined because `operator[]` returns by value rather than by reference for trivially copyable element types.
questions.explanation: Self-referencing insertion is explicitly required to work, and implementations achieve it by constructing into the new buffer first and only then destroying and deallocating the old one; `v.insert(v.begin(), v.back())` is required to work for the same reason. The dangling-reference answer describes what would happen with a naive implementation and is exactly what the guarantee rules out. Note this does *not* protect a `T* p = v.data()` you cached yourself.

questions.prompt: MSVC and folly's `fbvector` grow by 1.5 while libstdc++ and libc++ grow by 2. What is the argument for the smaller factor?
options: With a factor below φ ≈ 1.618 the sum of previously freed blocks eventually exceeds the next request, so a coalescing allocator can reuse that memory.
A factor of 1.5 performs fewer total element moves over n insertions than a factor of 2, roughly 2n versus 3n.
The standard mandates a factor strictly below φ, since a larger one would violate the amortized constant `push_back` requirement.
A factor of 2 loses the amortized constant guarantee once the buffer exceeds one page, because the allocator switches to `mmap`.
questions.explanation: Geometric growth with k=2 makes the sum 1+2+4+…+2^(i−1) always one short of the next request 2^i, so the freed blocks can never be recycled and the allocation walks forward through the address space; k<φ fixes that, but only for allocators that coalesce. The move-count answer is stated backwards — total moves are n·k/(k−1), so k=2 does 2n and k=1.5 does 3n, meaning the larger factor moves *less*. Neither factor is standardized; only amortized O(1), which any constant factor above 1 satisfies.

questions.prompt: What does `for (auto& x : src) { v.reserve(v.size() + 1); v.push_back(x); }` cost for n elements?
options: O(n) allocations and O(n²) element moves, because `reserve` grows capacity to exactly the requested value each time.
The same as a plain `push_back` loop, because `reserve` applies the implementation's geometric growth policy to the requested size.
One allocation, because the first `reserve` doubles capacity and every later request is then already satisfied.
O(n²) moves but only O(log n) allocations, because `reserve` rounds the request up to the next power of two.
questions.explanation: `reserve(n)` is specified to give capacity *at least* n and implementations give exactly n, so asking for `size()+1` every iteration defeats geometric growth entirely and reallocates on every push. The 'same as plain push_back' answer assumes `reserve` shares `push_back`'s growth policy, which is the precise misconception — `push_back` grows geometrically, `reserve` grows to order. Reserve once, up front, with the final count.

questions.prompt: A `vector` holds a million elements and you call `v.clear()`. What has happened to the memory, and how do you actually release it?
options: Capacity is unchanged and the buffer is still held; move-assigning an empty vector (or the `swap` idiom) actually frees it.
The buffer is deallocated and capacity drops to zero, so `clear()` alone is already sufficient.
Capacity is unchanged, but a following `shrink_to_fit()` is guaranteed by the standard to release the buffer.
Capacity is unchanged, and `reserve(0)` is the only operation that shrinks it back down.
questions.explanation: `clear()` runs destructors and sets size to zero; it never touches capacity, and neither does `pop_back` or `resize` down. The `shrink_to_fit` answer is the most tempting because it is *usually* honored — but it is an explicitly non-binding request, and even when honored it allocates a fresh buffer, copies, and invalidates everything. `v = std::vector<T>{};` is the modern release idiom.

questions.prompt: What is the status of `std::vector<int> v; v.reserve(10); v[0] = 42;`?
options: Undefined behavior: `reserve` changes only capacity, so no element exists at index 0; `resize(10)` is what creates elements.
Well-defined: `reserve` value-initializes the elements up to the requested capacity before returning.
Well-defined: `reserve(10)` sets both capacity and size to 10, so indices 0 through 9 are valid.
A compile error, because `operator[]` on a vector known to be empty is rejected as a constant-evaluated bounds check.
questions.explanation: `size()` is still 0 after `reserve`, so `v[0]` writes into raw, unconstructed storage — undefined behavior that happens to 'work' for `int` and corrupts things for non-trivial types. The value-initializing answer confuses `reserve` with `resize`, which is exactly the distinction being tested: `reserve` touches capacity, `resize` touches size. No compiler diagnoses this; `operator[]` is unchecked by design.

questions.prompt: `std::deque<Order> d; Order& o = d.front(); auto it = d.begin(); d.push_back(x);` — what is the state of `o` and `it`?
options: `o` is still valid; `it` may have been invalidated, since end insertion invalidates iterators but not references or pointers.
Both are still valid, since a `deque` never moves an existing element and its iterators hold a chunk pointer directly.
Both are invalidated, because appending may reallocate the map of chunk pointers and relocate the elements.
`o` is invalidated while `it` is still valid, since iterators are rebased onto the new map but references are not.
questions.explanation: This asymmetry is `deque`'s defining property and the single most-asked exam point about it: the elements themselves never move on an end insertion, but the map of chunk pointers may be reallocated, which is what the iterators depend on. 'Both valid' is the near-miss — a `deque` iterator carries four pointers including the map node, so a map reallocation breaks it. Note a *middle* insert or erase invalidates everything, references included.

questions.prompt: What is `std::deque`'s internal structure, and what does indexed access cost?
options: A dynamically allocated map of pointers to fixed-size chunks; `d[i]` is `map[i/K][i%K]`, so two indirections plus a division.
One contiguous buffer plus a head offset that wraps around, so `d[i]` is a masked add and a single load.
A doubly-linked list of fixed-size chunks, so `d[i]` walks chunks and costs O(n/K) rather than O(1).
Two vectors, one grown forwards and one backwards, so `d[i]` is a sign test plus one indirection into whichever half.
questions.explanation: The map-of-chunks layout is what buys O(1) at both ends *and* O(1) random access, at the price of two dependent loads and a real integer division — libstdc++ uses a 512-byte chunk, so K = max(1, 512/sizeof(T)) is often not a power of two and the shift optimization does not apply. The linked-chunks answer is tempting because it explains O(1) end insertion, but it would forfeit the O(1) indexing the standard requires.

questions.prompt: Why do `std::stack` and `std::queue` default to `deque` rather than `vector`?
options: Growth never relocates existing elements and never doubles memory, since only the map of chunk pointers is reallocated.
A `deque` is contiguous while a `vector` is not, so pushing and popping at the back is more cache-friendly.
`stack<T, std::vector<T>>` will not compile, because the adaptor requires the underlying container to provide `push_front`.
`deque::push_back` is amortized O(1) whereas `vector::push_back` is only O(log n) amortized under geometric growth.
questions.explanation: Avoiding the reallocation spike is the actual design rationale: a growing `deque` allocates one small chunk at a time and never has two copies of the data live. The `push_front` answer is doubly wrong — a stack never needs front insertion, and `stack<T, std::vector<T>>` not only compiles but is usually *faster* than the default because iteration and back access avoid the chunk indirection. `vector::push_back` is amortized O(1), not O(log n).

questions.prompt: Benchmarks repeatedly show `std::vector` beating `std::list` even for insert-in-the-middle workloads up to tens of thousands of elements. Why?
options: The list's O(1) insert is preceded by an O(n) traversal of dependent loads plus an allocation, while the vector's O(n) `memmove` streams at GB/s with perfect prefetching.
`list::insert` is secretly O(n) as well, because the container must renumber the nodes after the insertion point to keep `size()` O(1).
`std::list` allocates all of its nodes from one contiguous block, so the two containers differ only by a small constant factor.
The vector's insert avoids moving elements entirely, because the allocator grows the block in place and shifts nothing.
questions.explanation: The asymptotics compare the wrong operations: the O(1) insert only applies once you already hold the iterator, and getting there is a chain of pointer-chasing loads where the next address is unknown until the current node arrives, defeating the prefetcher and giving zero memory-level parallelism. The 'renumbering' answer invents a mechanism — `size()` is a single stored counter, updated in O(1). Vector's insert really does shift the tail; it is just extremely fast at it.

questions.prompt: What does `std::forward_list` give up relative to `std::list`?
options: `size()`, `back()`, and `push_back`, and its mutators are `_after` variants, since a singly-linked node cannot reach its predecessor.
`size()` and `splice`, since maintaining either requires walking backwards from the affected node to the list head.
`push_front` and `before_begin()`, since without a back pointer only the tail of a singly-linked list can be mutated cheaply.
`erase` and `insert` return values, which are `void` in `forward_list` because there is no way to name the following node.
questions.explanation: Every removal is `erase_after` and every insertion `insert_after` precisely because you cannot get from a node to the one before it, and `before_begin()` exists to give you a handle 'before' the first element so front insertion still works. The `push_front` answer inverts it: front operations are the *cheap* ones on a singly-linked list. The payoff is 8 bytes per node and `sizeof(std::forward_list<T>) == 8`.

questions.prompt: You splice one element from list `a` into list `b` while holding an iterator to that element. What is the cost and what happens to the iterator?
options: O(1) pointer surgery with no allocation and no element move; the iterator stays valid and now designates an element of `b`.
O(1) pointer surgery, but the iterator is invalidated because the element's owning container changed identity.
O(n) in the source list's length, since the element must be copy-constructed into `b` and destroyed in `a`.
O(1) for the relinking plus an allocation in `b`, because the destination must allocate a node before adopting the value.
questions.explanation: Splice relinks nodes and nothing else, so the element never moves in memory and the iterator keeps pointing at the same node — it simply belongs to the destination list afterwards, a guarantee unique to `list::splice`. The 'invalidated' answer is the intuitive guess and is what makes splice special. Note the *range* overload is O(1) only within one list; across lists it is O(distance) because `size()` must be maintained.

questions.prompt: `std::inplace_vector<T,N>` offers `push_back`, `try_push_back`, and `unchecked_push_back`. How do they behave when the container is full?
options: `push_back` throws `std::bad_alloc`, `try_push_back` returns `nullptr`, and `unchecked_push_back` is undefined behavior.
`push_back` returns `nullptr`, `try_push_back` throws `std::bad_alloc`, and `unchecked_push_back` silently discards the element.
All three throw `std::bad_alloc`; they differ only in whether they return a reference, a pointer, or `void` on success.
`push_back` falls back to a heap allocation, `try_push_back` returns `nullptr`, and `unchecked_push_back` truncates the container.
questions.explanation: The three-way split is the design point: the checked form reports overflow via an exception, the `try_` form via a null return with no exception machinery, and the unchecked form removes even the branch for a hot path that has already proven capacity. The 'falls back to the heap' answer describes small-vector optimization, not `inplace_vector` — the whole premise here is that no allocation ever happens, which is why overflow must be an error rather than a growth event.

questions.prompt: What does move construction cost for `std::inplace_vector<T,N>` compared with `std::vector<T>`?
options: The `inplace_vector` move is O(size) because each element must be moved individually; the `vector` move is O(1) because it steals three pointers.
Both are O(1): the `inplace_vector` swaps its internal buffer pointer just as `vector` swaps its heap pointer.
The `inplace_vector` move is O(1) whenever `T` is trivially copyable; the `vector` move is O(size) because elements must be reconstructed.
Both are O(size), because the standard requires a moved-from container to be left empty rather than in an unspecified state.
questions.explanation: The elements live inside the object, so there is no pointer to steal — moving means touching every element, which is the main price paid for zero indirection and zero allocation. The 'O(1) when trivially copyable' answer confuses cheapness with complexity: a trivial `inplace_vector` move is a fast `memcpy`, but it still copies `size` elements and grows linearly with `N`. That is why `inplace_vector` is wrong for large `N` or containers-of-containers.

questions.prompt: A small-vector implementation sets `data_ = inline_buf_` when in small mode. What breaks?
options: The object becomes self-referential, so it is not trivially relocatable and cannot be `memcpy`'d when an enclosing container reallocates.
Nothing: `memcpy` copies the inline buffer along with the pointer, so the copied pointer still designates the correct bytes.
Only `constexpr` use breaks, because a pointer into an object's own storage is not a valid constant expression at compile time.
Every element access gains an extra dependent load, since `data_` must be re-read from memory before the small/large mode is known.
questions.explanation: After a byte-wise relocation the copied `data_` still points at the *old* object's inline buffer, so the moved container reads freed storage — the classic SVO implementation bug, and the reason `llvm::SmallVector` compares `BeginX` against `getFirstEl()` instead of storing a self-pointer and `folly` tags its types `IsRelocatable`. The 'memcpy copies the pointer too' answer is exactly the wrong intuition: copying the pointer value is precisely the problem, since the address it holds is not relocated with it.

questions.prompt: A per-message field list holds at most 8 entries, a bound enforced by the wire protocol. Which container is the better fit and why?
options: `inplace_vector<T,8>`, since a hard bound removes the need for a heap fallback path, its branch, and the loss of trivial copyability.
A small-vector with N=8, since a bounded maximum is exactly the case where an inline buffer means it never allocates.
They are interchangeable here: `inplace_vector` is simply the standardized spelling of the same small-vector design.
`inplace_vector<T,8>`, since it falls back to the heap past 8 elements while a small-vector would truncate the message.
questions.explanation: SVO exists for 'usually small, occasionally unbounded'; when the maximum is genuinely bounded, the heap arm is dead weight that costs a discrimination branch and blocks trivial copyability, so the fixed-capacity container is strictly better. The small-vector answer is tempting because it also avoids allocating at these sizes — but it still carries the machinery for the case that can never occur. `inplace_vector` never falls back to the heap; overflow is an error, by design.

questions.prompt: You insert into the middle of a `vector` that has spare capacity, so no reallocation occurs. What is invalidated?
options: Iterators and references at or after the insertion point, plus `end()`, which is invalidated by every size change.
Only `end()`, since without reallocation the buffer address is unchanged and no element leaves its storage.
Iterators and references strictly before the insertion point, since the tail is what gets shifted into fresh storage.
Everything, because any insertion is specified to invalidate the whole container regardless of available capacity.
questions.explanation: The tail is shifted up by one slot by move-assignment, so every element from the insertion point onward now lives in different storage than before, while the prefix is untouched. 'Only `end()`' is the near-miss for people who remember that reallocation is the killer and stop there — the elements move even when the buffer does not. Reallocation widens this to *everything*, which is the case worth reserving against.

questions.prompt: What is the state of the container after `std::remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(), pred);` with no follow-up call?
options: `size()` is unchanged: the algorithm partitions the range, returns the new logical end, and leaves moved-from elements in the tail.
`size()` has shrunk by the number of matches, since `remove_if` erases them and returns the container's new `end()`.
The container is entirely unchanged, because algorithms operate through iterators and cannot modify the elements they visit.
The tail elements have been destroyed so `size()` has shrunk, though capacity is retained as with any other erasure.
questions.explanation: Algorithms only see iterators — they have no handle on the container and cannot change its size, so `remove_if` can only shuffle survivors forward and hand you the boundary. That is why the erase-remove idiom passes the returned iterator to `v.erase(it, v.end())`, and why `std::erase_if(v, pred)` (C++20) exists to make the whole thing one correct call. The 'size has shrunk' answers are the classic bug: the container still reports the old size and the tail holds moved-from junk.

questions.prompt: Other components hold raw pointers into your `std::vector<Order>`, which keeps growing. What is the recommended fix?
options: Hand out generational indices into a preallocated slab: an index survives every operation, is 4 bytes, and detects stale handles.
Switch to `std::deque`, whose references are guaranteed to survive any insertion or erasure anywhere in the container.
Switch to `std::list`, whose per-node allocation amortizes away under a pool and is the standard low-latency answer here.
Call `reserve` once at startup, which pins the buffer address and keeps the pointers valid however many orders arrive later.
questions.explanation: An index is not a memory address, so nothing a container does to its storage can invalidate it; adding a generation counter turns a stale handle into a detectable error instead of a use-after-free, and indices are smaller and shareable across processes. The `deque` answer overstates a real guarantee — references survive insertion at the *ends* only, and a middle insert or erase invalidates them. `reserve` only defers the problem until capacity is exceeded, and `list` buys stability at the cost of an allocation and a dependent load per element.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with `for (auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); ++it) if (pred(*it)) v.erase(it);` on a `std::vector`?
options: `erase` invalidates `it`, so the following `++it` is undefined behavior; write `it = pred(*it) ? v.erase(it) : std::next(it);` instead.
It is correct for `vector` but not for `list`, because only `vector::erase` returns an iterator to the following element.
It is well-defined but skips the element immediately after each match, so a run of two matches loses the second one.
It is correct, because `v.end()` is re-evaluated each iteration and `erase` leaves all iterators before it untouched.
questions.explanation: Erasing shifts the tail down, so the erased position and everything after it is invalidated and incrementing the dead iterator is UB, not merely a skipped element. The 'skips one element' answer is the tempting one because that *is* the symptom of the analogous bug on node-based containers where the iterator survives — here the iterator does not survive at all. For a `vector` the erase-remove idiom or `std::erase_if` is also O(n) rather than O(n²).
